integration.api: SAMSUNG'S OWN DOCUMENTATION UNDERSELLS THIS BADLY — the device is driveable over the LAN with no cloud and no app. Samsung publishes only two content paths: (1) the Samsung E-Paper mobile app for Android 10+/iOS 15+, which Samsung positions as LOCAL control including playlist creation, and (2) Samsung VXT, a cloud CMS sold separately. But the display also speaks Samsung's long-standing MDC (Multiple Display Control) protocol over TCP port 1515 (also RS-232C, and TCP-over-TLS with a PIN), and MDC includes the content commands that matter: set_content_download (which takes a content server address URL), launcher_play_via and launcher_url_address. The maintained open-source implementation states outright that it 'Supports ePaper displays (e.g., EM32DX)'. So his self-hosted app can host the image itself and tell the display to come and fetch it — a local pull he fully controls, no Samsung account, no VXT subscription.
integration.custom_software: No — Tizen 8.0 signage, no APK sideload, and he does not need it. All logic stays on his server; the display is a managed sink he addresses over TCP 1515.
integration.community: Small but decisive, and working on the actual hardware. (1) vgavro/samsung-mdc — Python, 109 stars, BSD-3-Clause, actively maintained, 84 MDC commands, explicitly documents ePaper/EM32DX support. (2) WeeJeWel/node-samsung-emdx — 43 stars, 13 forks, a purpose-built CLI for this exact display whose entire pitch is doing it 'without requiring cloud services or the Samsung app': `samsung-emdx show-image --mac <mac> --host <ip> --pin <pin> --image ~/Photos/Doggy.jpg`. That is one command from a shell script. A subagent reading the upstream issue threads (#20, #21, #22) reports the mechanism in detail — an image_url in a content.json pointing at the user's OWN local HTTP server, a URL length limit under 256 bytes, and a requirement that the content UUID change on every update or the panel will not refresh, with the feature landing in samsung-mdc v1.16.0 on 2025-10-07 after being validated against real EM32DX hardware. I did not fetch those issue threads myself, so treat the byte-level mechanism and version/date as unverified while the capability itself is verified from both repos. Two Home Assistant MDC integrations exist but neither handles images — for images, shell out to the CLI.
integration.notes: I INITIALLY RATED THIS CLOSED AND THAT WAS WRONG — flagging the reversal explicitly because it changes the recommendation. On vendor documentation alone the EM32DX looks like a phone-app appliance and therefore useless to him. In fact it is the ONLY device in this survey that combines unambiguous 3-year vendor staying power, a true 6-primary Spectra 6 panel, mainstream retail availability at $1,350, a genuinely handsome 17.9 mm frame with 200x200 VESA and a 200-day battery, AND a local, scriptable, cloud-free content path with working open-source client code. On his two decisive criteria together, nothing else here comes close. The residual risks are honest ones: the MDC content path is undocumented by Samsung and could change with a firmware update; 93 PPI is coarse for gigapixel detail; and Samsung's opaque on-device 'colour imaging algorithm' sits between his renderer and the pigment. Recommended primary development target, with the Philips Tableaux 25.3in as the higher-resolution alternative.

art_suitability.gamut_notes: Spectra 6 is a true multi-pigment 6-primary system, not a colour filter array, so it reads much closer to print than any Kaleido device here — E Ink's own language for the same panel generation in the Philips 32in claims saturation 'not previously seen in a reflective display, with a visual performance similar to high quality prints'. But 93 PPI at 31.5in is coarse: fine detail in gigapixel scans will be lost and dithering is unavoidable. No colour profile, Delta-E or gamut volume published. Samsung markets an 'advanced colour imaging algorithm', i.e. the device applies its own opaque colour mapping and dithering to whatever he sends — a real problem for controlled reproduction.
art_suitability.ghosting: Not documented by Samsung. Spectra 6 updates are slow full refreshes (Philips quotes 36 seconds on a comparable 25in panel), which is the favourable case for ghosting. No reviewer measurements found.
art_suitability.bit_depth: Not published. 6 primaries with device-side dithering; effective colour count claimed 54,600-77,000.

integration.api: No public REST API documented on the pages I could reach, but the platform is the point: Android 13 on a Rockchip RK3566 with 2 GB DDR4 and 16 GB eMMC, plus 10/100 Ethernet (RJ45), 802.11ac Wi-Fi, Bluetooth 5.1, USB and micro-USB. An Android device with Ethernet and USB is a general-purpose computer — he could plausibly run his own client on the display itself, listening on the LAN, with no vendor cloud in the loop.
integration.custom_software: Android 13 (RK3566), and the platform is demonstrably open to ADB — see the 25.3in sibling entry, where a hobbyist pushes image files over `adb push` into /storage/emulated/0/Pictures/ on a Tableaux and drives it with scrcpy. A subagent also read a commercial CMS vendor's certified-device install guide for THIS model documenting `adb install {application}.apk` over USB and then launching it, plus a factory-reset procedure; I did not fetch that document myself, so full APK sideload on the 32in specifically is reported rather than verified. Four commercial CMS vendors (PADS4, LiveSignage, viewneo, signageOS) integrate by sideloading their own APK, which is strong circumstantial evidence the mechanism is supported and supportable.
integration.community: No Tableaux-specific community — GitHub repo searches for 'philips tableaux' and 'philips epaper signage' return zero. The nearest thing is the single-hobbyist ADB workflow on the 13in Tableaux (see the 25.3in entry). Also worth noting: SICP, Philips' signage control protocol on TCP port 5000, has several open-source clients, but the SICP specification's platform table lists no ePaper model and neither Tableaux manual mentions SICP or port 5000 — and in any case SICP is control-only (input source, power, restart), with no command to set a browser URL or push an image, so it would not solve his problem even if present.
integration.notes: Excellent combination for his use case: Spectra 6 colour, zero standby power, PoE++ single-cable install, standard VESA, no CMS required (it boots into a local carousel reading a local directory), and an Android 13 SoC that accepts ADB. Remaining risks: unknown price through a quote-based AV channel, signage industrial design (12-18 mm bezel, not a picture frame), and the likelihood — based on the 13in first-hand report — that the documented USB-stick autoplay path is unreliable and ADB is the route that actually works.

integration.api: No vendor-documented API, but it has been fully reverse-engineered, and the result settles the question: there IS a usable programmatic path, and it is MANDATORILY CLOUD. A Home Assistant integration (mcuelenaere/ha-inkposter, declaring iot_class 'cloud_polling') ships two protocol documents derived from decompiling the Android APK plus TLS captures, validated against a real device. BLE (devices advertise as 'InkP-*') carries only commands — factory reset, settings including Wi-Fi provisioning, reboot, hello, FETCH and a ghosting cleaner — and there is NO BLE image-transfer command at all; BLE can only tell the frame to go fetch from the cloud. Images therefore go through api.inkposter.com: resize to the frame's exact resolution, POST /item/convert, poll /item/is-converted, POST /item/show-on-frame, then optionally trigger an immediate BLE fetch. Requests are HMAC-signed with a hardcoded Android client secret. No local HTTP, no mDNS, no LAN port, no SD/USB sideload.
integration.custom_software: No. Closed appliance; no platform disclosed. The only programmatic control is an unofficial client speaking to PocketBook's servers.
integration.community: Minimal and fragile: mcuelenaere/ha-inkposter is a single-author, 1-star, unlicensed integration created February 2026 and untouched since, and it is not in the HACS default repository. PocketBook can break it at will by rotating the hardcoded client secret. Model map in its BLE documentation covers W1330/Frame_13_3 (1200x1600), W2850/Frame_28_5 (2160x3060) and W3150/Frame_31_5 (2560x1440) — so both large models are addressed.
integration.notes: THE CONTRADICTION IS NOW RESOLVED, and the answer is nuanced rather than simply bad. The vendor page says the app uploads 'personal photography, illustrations, and artwork'; the launch release frames it as art-advisor-curated collections; a reader on The eBook Reader reported the Android app 'cannot transfer custom high-resolution images'. The reverse-engineered cloud API reconciles all three: custom images ARE supported as private items, but every image must be resized to the frame's EXACT resolution first — the API rejects non-standard resolutions with 'Model not detected by image resolution', which is almost certainly what that reader hit — and every image round-trips through api.inkposter.com to be converted server-side before it can be shown. So he CAN drive it from his own app; he just cannot do it without PocketBook's servers in the path, and he would be depending on a 1-star unlicensed integration and a hardcoded secret PocketBook can rotate. For a private archive of 3,400 works that is the wrong trade: it means uploading his collection to a third party's conversion service, with no local or offline fallback, on a device whose entire range is currently out of stock. Openness stays 'closed' because the decisive criterion — local network without vendor cloud — is a firm no.

integration.community: No third-party community code exists for this panel, but unlike the 25.3in it does not need any: THE INTERFACE IS THE WHOLE STORY. The 31.5in panel uses QSPI, which an ordinary microcontroller can drive, whereas the 25.3in uses Mini-LVDS and needs a TCON or FPGA. That single distinction is why Good Display can sell a $-level ESP32-S3 kit for the 31.5in and why no equivalent exists at 25.3in — and it makes the 31.5in the ONLY e-paper panel over 15 inches that a determined hobbyist can actually drive today.

integration.api: Completely open at the level he needs. The DEAM-315E1 kit is an ESP32-S3 board for exactly this panel, with an SD/TF card slot and 'SD-Card First Boot' auto-play on power-up (hot-swappable, explicitly 'ideal for offline environments'), a web-based Wi-Fi image transfer path for cloud-free updates, USB, QSPI to the panel, Arduino IDE compatibility and vendor-provided code examples for 'learning, testing, and secondary development'.
integration.custom_software: Yes — Arduino/ESP-IDF firmware he writes and owns. He could implement his own HTTP endpoint on the ESP32 and have his archive app POST a pre-dithered image directly, with no vendor software anywhere in the path.
integration.community: NONE, and he should go in expecting that. The Good Display / Waveshare ESP32 e-paper ecosystem is large but caps out well below this size: epdiy (1.9k stars) supports nothing above 13.3in, ESPHome's waveshare_epaper component tops out at 13.3in black-and-white with colour only to 7.3in, Inkplate's largest is 13.3in, and GitHub code searches for GDEP315C01 and DEAM-315E1 both return zero results. For this kit the vendor's own Arduino examples are the ONLY resource. That said, this remains the single viable >15in self-build in the survey, purely because the panel is QSPI rather than Mini-LVDS.
integration.notes: The openness benchmark and the honest fallback, and now the ONLY workable self-build path over 15 inches: a 31.5in Spectra 6 panel plus this ESP32-S3 kit gives him SD-card delivery, local Wi-Fi push, his own firmware and no vendor dependency beyond panel supply. What he gives up is the frame, battery management, enclosure, certification, warranty and any community to ask for help — real fabrication work with vendor sample code as the only map.

art_suitability.gamut_notes: Spectra 6 at 93.37 PPI, zero power in static display. Because he writes the firmware he owns the dithering and colour mapping entirely — no vendor imaging algorithm in the way. For a fine-art archive that is the strongest colour-control position available.

integration.api: THE BEST-DOCUMENTED INTEGRATION IN THIS SURVEY. Visionect publishes a full RESTful JSON management API at api.visionect.com covering /api/device, /api/device/{Uuid}, /api/session, /api/user and /api/config, with HMAC-SHA256 request signing modelled on AWS. Crucially there is a dedicated image-push endpoint: PUT /backend/{Uuid} on port 8081 accepts a multipart form with an 'image' field in PNG, JPG or GIF, and the HTTP backend writes that straight into the device framebuffer. Documented constraint that matters for his renderer: 'it will not be resized in any way to conform to the target screen size', and the image must be RGB palette with transparency disabled — so his app must emit exactly 2560x1440. A WebKit/HTML5 backend is also available if he would rather render a web page than an image.
integration.custom_software: Not on the display (it is a thin client), but the entire server side is his. The Visionect Software Suite runs self-hosted in Docker — official images visionect/visionect-server-v3, 100K+ pulls, last updated within the month, x86_64 and ARM64 (so a Raspberry Pi 5 or M-series Mac works), with Docker Compose alongside Redis and PostgreSQL 18+. Devices talk to the server on port 11113 and are pointed at it with the Visionect Configurator. Visionect's own Plans page confirms the route: the 'Essential Plan' is explicitly the on-premise self-hosted option, versus the managed Cloud and Signage plans.
integration.community: Real, documented, and already doing exactly what he wants. (1) Visionect itself publishes libpyvss on GitHub — an MIT-licensed Python client whose README includes a working image-upload example via the HTTP backend, though the repo is marked DEPRECATED and last saw commits around June 2022. (2) juicecultus/joan-dashboard (36 stars, MIT, 81 commits) renders weather/calendar/tasks/news/ART to greyscale images on the user's own machine and serves them to Visionect devices from a built-in HTTP image server on port 8888; its README states plainly that Joan devices point at getjoan.com by default and 'We replace that with a self-hosted VSS on your local network — no Joan subscription required.' (3) Adam7411/Joan-6-Visionect_Home-Assistant_EN documents a Proxmox/Docker self-hosted VSS stack plus a Home Assistant add-on exposing services to push custom URLs or LOCAL IMAGES and entities for battery/connection state. Buying Visionect hardware and cutting the cloud out entirely is established practice, not a theory. (4) MOST RELEVANT OF ALL: graiz/newsprint — 252 stars, MIT — is built specifically for 'a 32" eInk place & play display from Visionect', fetching newspaper front pages, converting them and displaying them; it confirms his exact use case works on this exact model, while also confirming the dependency, since its README states 'The display itself is not standalone, it's a thin client and requires the Visionect software to act as an HTML rendering engine.' (5) elidickinson/newsvision — 44 stars — does the same for the 32in using libpyvss's set_http(uuid, img) to PUT a PNG. (6) Finally, a genuinely licence-free escape hatch exists but not yet for this size: timeframe/ha-addon (854 stars) contains a clean-room reimplementation of the Visionect PV3 device wire protocol on TCP port 11114, so displays talk directly to the user's own server with no VSS and no licence at all — but it targets the Place & Play 13 / Joan 13 Pro at 1600x1200 and is flagged experimental, NOT the 32in.
integration.notes: THREE CAVEATS, AND TOGETHER THEY ARE PROBABLY DISQUALIFYING FOR THIS PROJECT — I am revising down from my first pass. First, the panel is MONOCHROME 16-grey, which for a colour fine-art archive is close to fatal on its own. Second, THE LICENCE IS A HARD GATE, not a soft cost: Visionect's own installation documentation states 'The VSS_LICENSE_ID environmental variable must be set in order for the VSS to function. Without a proper value for the license, the devices will not be able to operate.' So a self-hosted install does NOT survive a lapsed licence — the displays stop working. Docker Hub records hard enforcement from v7.7.0. On price, visionect.com/pricing returns HTTP 404, but a developer who deployed Visionect displays at 6in, 10in, 13in and 32in reports that around 2021 'Visionect started charging a $7/mo per-device fee to run their backend software on premises with Docker, after years of it being free to use' — i.e. roughly $84/year per frame, forever, on hardware he already owns. Third, and most damning, that same first-hand source evaluated this exact 32in panel and REJECTED it: it 'used an outdated lower-contrast panel and its resolution was too low to render text smoothly'. He bought a BOOX Mira Pro 25.3in instead. So the best-documented API in the survey sits on the worst-regarded large panel behind a kill-switch licence.

art_suitability.gamut_notes: No colour at all. 16 grey levels at 94 PPI. For a colour archive this is fundamental; for high-quality monochrome it is workable but coarse, and every image needs careful tone mapping and error-diffusion dithering to 16 levels — squarely in his app's wheelhouse, since the API accepts a pre-rendered exact-size PNG. HOWEVER a developer who bought and deployed this exact 32in unit describes it as 'an outdated lower-contrast panel' whose 'resolution was too low to render text smoothly' — the only independent hands-on assessment of any large panel in this survey, and it is negative.
art_suitability.ghosting: Vendor documents 750 ms full-screen and 100 ms partial refresh — very fast for e-paper. Ghosting on image change is not documented and I found no reviewer measurement.

integration.api: Genuinely documented and substantial: a RESTful JSON API with HMAC-SHA256 authentication on a self-hosted server (port 8081). Endpoints include /api/device, /api/session, /api/user, /api/config, /api/live/device/{Uuid}/image, /api/devicestatus/{Uuid} and /backend/{Uuid} for HTTP image backend uploads. Capabilities include pushing HTML content to displays, controlling dithering method and bit-depth encoding, device/battery/temperature monitoring, batch reboot and firmware flashing.
integration.custom_software: The display is a thin client; all rendering happens server-side in a WebKit session on your own server, so 'custom software' is simply whatever web application you host. The client's existing self-built app could drive this essentially unchanged.
integration.community: No homebrew community found, but a proper documentation site (docs.visionect.com) with Installation, Production deployment, Requirements, Networking & Security, Firmware upgrades, Components and Display tiling sections.
integration.notes: Highest integration openness of any commercially supported >15 in product in this survey, and the only one where a self-hosted server pushing images is the DESIGNED architecture rather than a workaround: you install the Software Suite on your own machine, the display polls it, and the documented API includes explicit control over dithering method and bit depth - precisely the levers that matter for rendering gigapixel art to e-paper. THE DISQUALIFIER for this client is that it is monochrome. 16-level greyscale at 94 PPI is excellent for text and line work and useless for colour reproductions. Worth flagging anyway for two reasons: it is the reference example of what good openness looks like, so it is the right yardstick to hold colour vendors against; and if Visionect ever ships a Spectra 6 model it would instantly become the leading candidate. One caution: the docs recommend their cloud-managed hosting 'for the best security and the latest features', so self-hosting is supported but is the secondary path, and a licence is required either way.

Community: seanhub2000/bloomin8-canvas-desktop-app (native macOS manager, updated hours before this survey), mrud/bloomin8-cli (Node/JS CLI with Spectra 6 dithering and multi-device control), jacobstim/bloomin8-python, moifort/bloomin8 (Swift local server), Dopiz/bloomin8-canvas-skills (LAN control), mistrsoft/bloomin8_bt_wake (BLE wake), gabe-sky/bloomin8-simulacrum, PhilWheat/Bloomin8HermesSkill.

Vendor markets a 'Fully Local Solution' explicitly: an SD card slot where you drop images pre-resized to panel resolution, plus a Home Assistant custom integration that uploads and displays 'images 100% locally over your home Wi-Fi network. No third-party servers'. CAVEAT: the vendor's cloud/mobile app carries an AI-generation subscription ('Premium plans offer up to 300 generations monthly'), but that is orthogonal to local image push. SECOND CAVEAT: the GitHub account github.com/bloomin8 has zero public repositories - the real code lives under the ARPOBOT-BLOOMIN8 org, so do not conclude from the bare vendor name that nothing is published. The vendor FAQ does not document the API; the API contract is effectively defined by the HA component source, which is a single-vendor dependency risk if they stop publishing it.

integration.community: THE BEST-SUPPORTED DEVICE IN THIS SURVEY BY COMMUNITY DEPTH — at least four independent working control tools plus a ready-made dashboard platform. (1) mira-js (ipodnerd3019/mira-js) — GPL-3.0 Node.js library and CLI, 63 stars, controlling refresh mode, contrast, speed, dither mode, white/black filters and mode presets over USB HID (VID 0416, PID 5020; hidraw/libusb) on Linux/macOS/Windows for both Mira 13.3 and Mira Pro 25.3. (2) elithper/miractl — Python/hidapi, 10 stars, GPL-3.0, EXPLICITLY tested on both 'Boox Mira 13.3" and Boox Mira Pro 25.3"', controlling refresh mode, speed 1-7, contrast 0-15, dither mode, filters, cool/warm front light and antiflicker algorithms, with five presets (speed/text/image/video/read), tested on Linux, Mac and Windows under Python 3.11 (note the earlier sourcehut URL for this project returned HTTP 502; the GitHub repo is live). (3) clarkema/miractl — Rust, GPL-3.0, with a Nix flake. (4) rynom99/mira-cli and martin-paulus/boox-mira-cli. All require a udev rule; most were last touched in 2023, which is fine for a stable HID protocol. AND (5) timeframe/ha-addon — 854 stars, PolyForm Noncommercial, actively developed (273 commits), a Home Assistant e-paper dashboard platform that explicitly supports the 'Boox Mira Pro 25.3"' with REAL-TIME WEBSOCKET UPDATES. That is a maintained, popular, off-the-shelf integration for this exact display.
integration.notes: The most open category in the survey and the least glamorous: an e-paper MONITOR has no cloud, no account, no ToS gate and no vendor CMS, because it is only a display sink. Crucially — and unlike DASUNG — it holds an image from HDMI alone with no keepalive daemon, and its physical front-panel buttons (refresh button, function button, scroll wheel) let a human clear ghosting without any host software at all. A first-hand owner of both a Mira Pro and a DASUNG colour unit reports the Mira Pro's 'Input is just HDMI, so works on Linux without issue' and that all relevant settings are configurable from the front panel; the vendor Linux client is settings-only and never needed for the picture. The trade-off remains a permanently attached powered host, continuous mains draw, a monitor stand and bezel, and a front light. Lowest-risk integration target of anything here; wrong industrial design for a wall-hung artwork.

Weakest colour technology here for reproductions; the Spectra 6 devices look materially closer to print. The CFA also cuts reflectance, which is why a front light is fitted.

integration.custom_software: THE DEAL-BREAKER FOR AN ALWAYS-ON ART FRAME. DASUNG's current 'Revolutionary' generation (Paperlike 253 and Paperlike Color) requires a continuously running USB keepalive just to KEEP AN IMAGE ON SCREEN. The independent Linux driver for the 253 states it plainly: 'The monitor turns off the image after ~5 seconds unless it receives 5FF52001000000000000A0FA at least every 4-5 seconds', and its troubleshooting section reads 'Image disappears after a few seconds: The keepalive loop stopped.' So the display needs HDMI/DP for video AND a USB serial connection with a daemon running forever — versus the BOOX Mira Pro, which holds an image from HDMI alone. Worse, mode/contrast/refresh switching on the 253 from Linux is explicitly UNSOLVED in that project: the register values are undocumented. Layered on top is DASUNG's own documented limitation that a 'Paperlike client' (Mac V2.0 / Windows V2.0) is needed for full refresh-mode control and that 'On Linux, only extended display mode is supported', plus a warning that adapters/dongles cannot output video stably.
integration.community: Present but weaker and more fragmented than BOOX's, and split across two incompatible control transports by hardware generation: the older Paperlike HD/HD-FT used I2C DDC over the video cable (leoluk/paperlike-go, 34 stars; lilydjwg/paperlike-i2c), while the current Revolutionary generation uses USB serial over a CH340 bridge (dnsandmann/Dasung-Paperlike-253-Linux-Driver, 3 stars, MIT, tested on Linux Mint 22 and NixOS 24.11; roflecopter/paperlike13k_linux; cpmetz/dasung253). Nothing has full mode control on the 253.
integration.notes: Downgraded from 'open' to 'partly-open' on the keepalive evidence. A display that blanks after five seconds without a USB heartbeat is the wrong foundation for an unattended wall-hung artwork: it converts a passive frame into a device with a mandatory always-running host daemon and a second cable, and if the daemon dies the artwork vanishes. Combined with unsolved mode control on Linux and DASUNG's own Linux de-featuring, there is no reason to prefer this over the BOOX Mira Pro at a similar price. The 50Hz refresh headline is irrelevant to a static art frame.

integration.api: No public REST API found. Platform: Android 11 on Rockchip PX30, 2 GB LPDDR3, 16 GB eMMC. Connectivity is the strongest of any frame-style device here — 10/100 Ethernet (RJ45), dual-band Wi-Fi, USB Type-A, micro-USB AND a microSD card slot. The microSD plus USB-A gives a genuine offline fallback delivery path the consumer art frames lack.
integration.custom_software: YES — CONFIRMED ON REAL TABLEAUX HARDWARE, which upgrades this from 'plausible' to 'done by someone'. ADB appears to be open out of the box on the USB service port: avulanov/photoframe documents a working workflow on a Philips Tableaux 13BDL4150IW (the same Android 11 Tableaux platform, smaller panel) from macOS — `brew install scrcpy android-platform-tools`, `adb devices`, `adb -s <serial> shell`, and critically `adb -s <serial> push *original.bmp /storage/emulated/0/Pictures/`. scrcpy is used because the panels have no touch input. A subagent additionally read a commercial CMS vendor's install guide for the 32BDL5150I documenting `adb install {application}.apk` over USB followed by launching it — i.e. full third-party APK sideload — but I did not fetch that document myself, so APK install is reported-and-plausible while `adb push` of image files is verified. NO evidence of network ADB (adb connect <ip>:5555) on any Philips signage display — every source uses USB, so assume a cable is needed for provisioning.
integration.community: Thin but real and directly on point. avulanov/photoframe (C, 1 star) is one hobbyist running a photo frame on a Tableaux by pushing bitmaps over ADB into /storage/emulated/0/Pictures/ with a config.xml alongside. GitHub repo searches for 'philips tableaux', 'tableaux epaper' and code search for '25BDL4050I' return zero — so there is no community, just an existence proof. Note also that the 854-star timeframe/ha-addon project names a Philips Tableaux model as a candidate cheaper Android alternative to its $2,000 Boox Mira Pro but has not implemented it.
integration.notes: 145 PPI at 25.3in makes this the highest-resolution COLOUR e-paper surface actually purchasable today — 1.55x the linear detail of the 93 PPI Spectra 6 panels — and it has microSD, USB-A and Ethernet, with ADB confirmed working on the platform. TWO IMPORTANT CAVEATS FROM THE SAME FIRST-HAND SOURCE. First, the documented USB-stick autoplay route does NOT work in practice: 'According to the manual, photos can be placed in /Pictures folder on the USB drive. However, it does not work' — the device kept demanding a USB with Pictures, which is precisely why he fell back to adb push. So treat SD/USB as documented-but-unreliable and ADB as the dependable path. Second, and useful for art: he recommends letting Philips' own on-device dithering do the conversion, because it knows the panel palette, which he infers by inspection to be about 8 base colours (black, white, red, green, blue, light blue, magenta, yellow). That is a much smaller effective palette than the '60,000 colours' marketing figure implies, and it is the single most important art-suitability fact about this device.

art_suitability.gamut_notes: Philips claims 60,000 colours on E Ink Advanced Colour ePaper at 145 PPI — the best PPI-plus-full-colour combination purchasable. BUT TREAT THE COLOUR CLAIM SCEPTICALLY: the one person who has actually driven a Tableaux panel himself infers the device palette is roughly 8 base colours (black, white, red, green, blue, light blue, magenta, yellow), with the 60,000 figure achieved by device-side dithering rather than by 60,000 addressable states. ACeP is generally less saturated than Spectra 6, though far better than Kaleido. No colour profile, gamut volume or Delta-E published. Practical implication: send full-resolution images and let the device dither, since its dithering knows the real palette and his renderer does not.
art_suitability.ghosting: Philips documents a 36-second image update — a slow full refresh, the best case for a clean static image, and it eliminates partial-refresh ghosting as a concern.

integration.api: Open in principle — he writes the driver — but with a HARD PRACTICAL BLOCKER I did not appreciate on first pass. E Ink's own listing warns that 'Driving Board is not included in the display module package' and directs buyers to a Vision Driving Board sold separately. That matters more than it sounds, because 25.3in panels at this size use a Mini-LVDS interface and REQUIRE a TCON or FPGA — an MCU cannot drive them. This is precisely why 25.3in panels only ever appear inside FPGA-based products (BOOX Mira, DASUNG, Modos), and it is why there is no hobbyist path here.
integration.custom_software: In principle anything; in practice he would need to design or buy a Mini-LVDS TCON and write the waveform driver, which is FPGA-level work rather than Arduino-level work.
integration.community: NONE. This is the corrected finding. GitHub code searches for the large Good Display part numbers return zero; epdiy — the main open-source e-paper controller project, 1.9k stars — tops out at ED133UT2, 13.3in 1600x1200, and supports nothing above 13.3in; ESPHome's waveshare_epaper component tops out at 13.3in and only in black and white (colour caps at 7.3in); and Modos Glider, despite the widely-repeated claim, cannot drive a 25.3in panel (see that entry). There is no open-source code driving any e-paper panel over 15 inches.
integration.notes: RETRACTING AN EARLIER RECOMMENDATION. I initially proposed this panel plus a Modos Glider as the ideal fine-art build; that combination does not work, because Glider cannot reach the required pixel rate and 25.3in panels need Mini-LVDS anyway. Rated openness 'unknown' rather than 'open' because although nothing forbids him from driving it, no documented path exists that he could actually follow. The resolution and PPI are still not on the listing, and that remains the highest-value unknown in the survey — a 25.3in Spectra 6 at 3200x1800 would be the best fine-art e-paper surface in existence — but even if the answer is favourable he cannot currently drive it. If he wants a self-build, use the 31.5in QSPI panel instead (next entry), which IS MCU-drivable.

integration.api: No vendor API - this is a raw mini-LVDS panel. You supply the driving stack. Two documented routes: (1) Good Display's own 25.3" TCON board plus Android system motherboard, which ships with an SDK and takes images from a USB drive prepared by a Windows tool, or over Wi-Fi/Bluetooth; (2) the open-source Modos Caster/Glider FPGA controller, whose documentation explicitly covers the LVDS signalling used on 'higher resolution panels (such as 25.3" ones ...)'.
integration.custom_software: Entirely yours. Nothing to sideload around - you own the whole stack from framebuffer to waveform.
integration.community: Modos Caster/Glider (CERN-OHL, GitLab/GitHub mirrors) is the only open controller documented as reaching this panel class. EPDiy, the other well-known open ESP32 e-paper driver, tops out around 13.3" and its README lists nothing above ~7.8-13.3" and no Spectra 6 support.
integration.notes: This is the highest-resolution >15 in colour e-paper panel found anywhere in this survey at 163 PPI - substantially sharper than every 31.5" option (~93 PPI) and sharper than the 28.5" A2 panels (~131 PPI). For a fine-art application that is the single most important spec, and it makes this panel the best raw substrate available. Two hard caveats. FIRST, an important and under-appreciated compatibility risk: Caster's own documentation says it 'supports electrophoretic display panels with parallel I/F (Eink, OED and DES)' and is 'compatible with both monochrome and color-filter-array based screens'. Spectra 6 is NOT a colour-filter-array device - it is a four-pigment microcup system needing its own multi-pass waveform set. So Caster driving this panel's LVDS timing is documented, but Caster rendering correct Spectra 6 COLOUR is not, and would likely need new waveform work. Treat 'open controller drives the 25.3" in full colour' as INFERENCE, not fact, until demonstrated. SECOND, Glider's README notes a constraint that X resolution multiplied by Y resolution must be a multiple of 128; 3200 x 1800 = 5,760,000, which divides by 128 exactly (45,000), so this panel does satisfy it. The pragmatic route for a determined builder is Good Display's own TCON plus Android motherboard with SDK, which is a known-good colour stack, and to treat the open FPGA path as a research project.

art_suitability.gamut_notes: 163 PPI, 4,096 colours, 85% NTSC, ~30:1 contrast, anti-glare glass. Best pixel density above 15 in that this survey found. Because Spectra 6 reaches intermediate colours by dithering, high PPI matters disproportionately here - dither noise is what limits perceived quality, and 163 PPI hides it far better than 93 PPI. Operating range 0-50 C; storage -25 to 60 C.
art_suitability.ghosting: Not documented by the vendor. Spectra 6 large-format modules generally require full-panel refresh for image changes; the finished products built on this panel quote <=15 s full refresh, which implies a multi-pass waveform and therefore visible transition activity rather than instant swap.
art_suitability.bit_depth: 4,096 addressable colours quoted at panel level (equivalent to 12-bit total via dithered primaries, not per-channel)

integration.notes: Best openness-per-unit-of-corporate-durability trade in the whole slice, and the most under-recognised vendor found. Geniatech is a 27-year-old Shenzhen ARM embedded design house with its own 30,000+ sq m factory, 100+ R&D engineers and 2,000+ claimed clients - not a frame startup - and it sells all three interesting sizes (25.3, 28.5, 31.5) as complete units with an Android SoC, a TCON it designs itself, and an explicitly open API/SDK. The EPC2530 in particular pairs the 163 PPI 25.3 in panel with Android 11, which on paper is the single best combination of image quality and drivability found above 15 in. Rated partly-open only because none of the API documentation is public - everything is behind a sales conversation, cloud CMS is the default content path, and local-only operation is not affirmatively documented. Worth a direct enquiry: ask for the SDK docs, whether the CMS can be self-hosted or bypassed, and whether APK sideloading is permitted. Downside for a private client: this is a B2B signage vendor, so expect MOQ friction, no consumer support, and industrial rather than gallery-grade finish (though the EPC3200 is full metal).

integration.api: Documented and published. glider-api is a 'Common API for interacting with e-ink displays' over USB HID with Python, Rust and C bindings; commands include set_mode() for per-region refresh-mode selection and multi-zone layouts. Modos also ships a C API for screen and mode selection. Caveat from the repo itself: not yet installable as a Python wheel or Rust crate - build from source.
integration.custom_software: Fully. Flow presents as a standard USB-C DisplayPort monitor to Linux, macOS and Windows, so any local application drives it with no vendor involvement whatsoever. Firmware source, changelogs and versioned releases are published; standalone operation is supported via the on-board STM32H750.
integration.community: Real and active. Public issue tracker, Discord, Matrix, Mastodon, Bluesky. Community contributions already landing - a member implemented Atkinson dithering on Flow, tuning error diffusion and artefact reduction, which is directly relevant to image quality on e-paper. Conference talk record spanning FOSDEM 2024, Supercon 2024, Latch-up 2024 and FOSDEM 2026.
integration.notes: Openness here is in a different league from every commercial vendor in this survey - CERN-OHL licensed hardware, published schematics, open gateware, a real host API, and an as-a-monitor path that needs no integration work at all. This is the clearest instance of the pattern the brief asked to be called out: Modos wins criterion 2 outright and loses criterion 1 badly, being a two-person company. THE SIZE PROBLEM, stated plainly: the Dev Kit's Glider Mega Adapter covers 4.3" to 13.3" only - the published adapter list ends at 13.3" (ES133UTx/ED133UTx/EC133UJ1) and 11.3" (ED113TCx), and the campaign says 'Compatible with a wide range of screens - from 6-inch up to 13.3-inch'. Flow itself is marked 'Works With Other Panels: No'; only the Dev Kit is 'Yes'. So there is no ready-made Modos product above 15 in. The path that exists is: buy the 13" Dev Kit for its Caster driver board, and drive a 25.3" LVDS panel per the Glider documentation - a bring-up project, not a purchase.

art_suitability.gamut_notes: 300 PPI is far beyond anything available above 15 in, but Kaleido 3 is a colour-filter-array over a monochrome panel: colour resolution is a fraction of the mono resolution and saturation is markedly lower than Spectra 6. For colour art reproduction Kaleido 3 is the weaker technology; for monochrome/graphite/etching reproduction at 300 PPI it is the best option in this entire survey. Amber-tinted frontlight is available, which is a colour-accuracy negative for art viewing.
art_suitability.ghosting: Actively engineered against - hybrid binary-then-16-level-greyscale mode updates fast first and refines to greyscale as the image settles, explicitly to minimise latency and visual flashing. Hardware Bayer, blue-noise and error-diffusion dithering with no added latency. Vendor addresses panel wear directly and states fast refresh does not increase total refresh cycles.
art_suitability.bit_depth: Binary, 4-level and 16-level greyscale output modes; 4,096 colours with 16 grey levels on the colour model

devices.panel: Panel-agnostic EPD controller (Caster FPGA gateware on a Xilinx Spartan-6 LX16 + STM32H750 firmware) for panels without an integrated TCON. ACTUAL supported sizes top out at 13.3in — see integration notes for the correction to the widely-repeated '4in to 42in' claim.
devices.colour: Depends on the panel fitted — monochrome, Kaleido and Spectra/Gallery panel types are addressed by the design
devices.availability: Crowd Supply campaign, funded against a $110,000 goal, crowdfunding deadline 2025-09-18. The KITS SOLD ARE 6in ($199) and 13.3in ($599) — both under his 15in threshold — so for a large frame he buys the controller and supplies his own 25.3in/31.2in/42in panel. Ship dates have moved: IEEE Spectrum and CNX both reported January 2026 for backers, explicitly not guaranteed, and later coverage indicates orders now ship around 28 July 2026. I could NOT verify current status — crowdsupply.com returned HTTP 403 on the campaign page and the shipping update — so treat the ship date as unverified.
devices.power: Board-level; USB-C.
devices.dimensions: Controller board; enclosure is the builder's problem.

integration.api: Architecturally the most open thing in the survey. Glider is a genuine video-input EPD controller: USB-C DisplayPort alt-mode (PTN3460) and micro-HDMI/DVI (ADV7611) in, e-paper out, up to 75 Hz — a record for e-paper, against ~10 Hz typical. It presents as a HID device so no host driver is needed, and modes are host-software runtime controllable. A panel behind it becomes an ordinary MONITOR to his renderer, with the controller doing waveforms and hardware Bayer / blue-noise / error-diffusion dithering.
integration.custom_software: Fully. Open hardware (KiCad), open STM32H750 firmware and open Caster FPGA gateware (Xilinx Spartan-6 LX16, DDR3-800 framebuffer), all on GitHub with extensive documentation. 2.5k stars, 166 commits on main. Mirrored from gitlab.com/zephray/glider.
integration.community: 2.5k GitHub stars plus coverage in IEEE Spectrum, Hackaday, CNX Software and Notebookcheck.
integration.notes: I HAD THIS WRONG IN AN EARLIER PASS AND AM CORRECTING IT EXPLICITLY, BECAUSE THE ERROR IS WIDESPREAD AND WOULD HAVE COST HIM MONEY. Press coverage and summaries repeat that Glider 'supports 4in to 42in E-Ink displays', which reads as a licence to pair it with a 25.3in or 31.5in panel. It is a misreading. Reading the full raw README, that size range comes from an APPENDIX 'Screen List' carrying its own explicit disclaimer: 'This is a list of all E-ink screens that have public information available, not a list of screens that's compatible with the Glider.' In the same list the largest panel marked Tested is ED050SU3 at 5.0in, and the compatibility table's largest entries are 13.3in TTL panels. The Glider Mega Adapter covers 4.3in-13.3in only. The arithmetic settles it from the README's own figures: a 3200x1800 25.3in panel needs 364 MP/s at 60 Hz and 522 MP/s at 85 Hz, while Glider's maxima are 224 MP/s over DisplayPort, 230 MP/s over MIPI/LVDS, 165 MP/s over DVI and 360 MP/s from DDR3-800 x16 memory — so it is 1.6x to 2.3x short, and the README notes greyscale rendering wants 85 Hz. CONCLUSION: as of 2026-08 there is NO open-source controller that can drive a >15in e-paper panel. The elegant self-build I had proposed — Glider plus a 25.3in Spectra 6 module — does not work today. Keep the entry on file because the design is aware of large panels (the README documents that 25.3in panels use LVDS signalling with a DRST sequence, and the 16-pin connector adds LVDS support), so a future revision could close the gap.

art_suitability.gamut_notes: Whatever the fitted panel supports, with hardware error-diffusion dithering in the controller — up to 133 MP/s with dithering on. He controls the dithering pipeline, which is the thing every finished product hides behind a proprietary imaging algorithm.
art_suitability.ghosting: Controller-level waveform control. The project's premise is low-latency e-paper so fast modes will ghost, but for a static frame he can drive clean full refreshes.

sources.what_it_supports: Open-source e-ink monitor controller with Caster FPGA EPDC gateware; up to 133 MP/s with error-diffusion dithering, >200 MP/s without; dev kits at 13.3in 1600x1200 and 6in 1404x1072; 2.5k stars, 166 commits; mirror of gitlab.com/zephray/glider

THE CORRECTION. Raw README confirms the appendix Screen List disclaimer verbatim — 'This is a list of all E-ink screens that have public information available, not a list of screens that's compatible with the Glider' — that the largest panel marked Tested is ED050SU3 at 5.0in 800x600, and the pixel-rate ceilings: DisplayPort/PTN3460 224 MP/s, MIPI with 1.05Gbps LVDS 230 MP/s, DVI/ADV7611 165 MP/s, DDR2/3-800 x16 360 MP/s; and that a 3200x1800 25.3in panel needs 364 MP/s at 60Hz and 522 MP/s at 85Hz — proving Glider cannot drive a 25.3in panel today

vendors.name: AUO Corporation and AUO Display Plus (ADP)
vendors.corporate_form: AUO Corporation is listed on the Taiwan Stock Exchange. AUO Display Plus is a wholly-owned subsidiary. The large-format ePaper module JV with E Ink is a separate company, ADP 51% / E Ink 49%.
vendors.ownership: Publicly held; ADP wholly owned by AUO
vendors.funding: Public markets. The E Ink JV has NT$390 million of paid-in capital.
vendors.revenue_scale: FY2025 consolidated revenue NT$281.39 billion (+0.4% YoY), net profit attributable to owners NT$6.84 billion, basic EPS NT$0.90, gross margin 11.5%, OPERATING MARGIN -0.4%, EBITDA margin 10.2%. The company states profitability 'improved significantly in 2025 compared with the previous year, turning losses into gains'.
vendors.hardware_track_record: Decades as one of the world's large TFT-LCD makers. ADP brings an existing smart-retail and digital-signage customer base. Strategic partnership with E Ink to develop large-size colour ePaper announced April 2024, escalating to the JV term sheet in April 2025 with mass production targeted from Q4 2025. ADP also manufactures the 31.5in aecoPost e-paper signage unit for StellarLink in Japan.
vendors.abandonment_history: Not researched behaviourally. The relevant signal is financial: AUO's core panel business runs at a NEGATIVE full-year operating margin (-0.4% in 2025) and its net profit is thin relative to revenue (NT$6.84bn on NT$281bn, about 2.4%). This is a low-margin commodity manufacturer whose 2025 profit was a recovery from prior-year losses, not a franchise.
vendors.distributor_footprint: B2B panel and module supply; ADP sells into smart retail and signage channels globally.
vendors.rationale: AUO is not going away — a listed NT$281bn-revenue panel maker — but its economics are the opposite of E Ink's: razor-thin and cyclical, with a full-year operating loss in 2025. For this buyer AUO matters indirectly and positively: the ADP/E Ink JV is the single most important structural development for large-format e-paper supply, because it moves 30-40 inch module assembly out of E Ink's own constrained lines into a company with industrial-scale manufacturing and an existing signage channel. That makes large modules more commodity-like and reduces the chance any one frame brand's supply simply evaporates. The caveat: a business at -0.4% operating margin exits product lines, and the JV is only 51%-owned by ADP with NT$390 million of capital — trivially small in AUO terms, hence trivially cheap for AUO to walk away from if large-format ePaper does not scale. One further open question: I could not confirm whether the April 2025 term sheet has converted into a definitive agreement.

vendors.rationale: OUT OF SCOPE TODAY — Aura Ink is 13.3in — but this is the company most likely to still be patching frame firmware in 2029, and the client should keep a standing watch on it. Roughly US$39-47 million raised from named tier-one investors, 997,000 frames shipped, 3 million app users, about 50 patents, 14 years in the category, and a deliberate subscription-free position on its e-paper debut. If Aura ever ships above 15 inches it displaces most of the medium and low tier in this file on staying power alone. vendors.name: BLOOMIN8 / arpobot
vendors.country: Australia (Sydney — D9/161 Arthur Street, Homebush West 2140) and China (Shenzhen — 307 Chongwen Park, Nanshan District)
vendors.corporate_form: NO LEGAL ENTITY NAME PUBLISHED ANYWHERE. The site footer is a bare '(c) 2026 BLOOMIN8'. A US support line (+1 833-986-3700) is listed.
vendors.ownership: Not disclosed. Six named team members: Francis (creator), Eric (supply chain), Piper (marketing), Evan and Linda (engineering).
vendors.funding: Crowdfunding. The BLOOMIN8 EinkCanvas Kickstarter raised AU$2,397,443 from 2,272 backers against an AU$30,000 goal, campaign 2025-03-18 to 2025-04-27 (a secondary source reports the total as 'over $1.65M', which is consistent as the USD equivalent). Launch marketing by The Crowdfunding Formula (TCF). No institutional investors disclosed.
vendors.revenue_scale: Roughly AU$2.4M crowdfunding plus ongoing direct sales across 13.3 in and 28.5 in SKUs; a 10 in sub-USD-200 model was announced for CES 2026.
vendors.headcount: Not disclosed. Self-described as 'smart home experts'.
vendors.hardware_track_record: Second crowdfunded product. Prior product was the Arpobot Smart Shade, a Matter-over-Thread smart home device, with '600+ backers fulfilled from previous Kickstarter campaign' claimed on the current campaign page. For the EinkCanvas itself, the 13.3 in model has shipped and is in retail, an extensive app version history is shown, development on the 4 in Spectra 6 display is dated to June 2024, and the 28.5 in large model is listed with 'Expected shipping starts August 2026' - i.e. the large SKU is the tail end of an 18-month fulfilment. 20 campaign updates, last activity 2026-07-31.
vendors.abandonment_history: TWO FINDINGS, ONE SERIOUS. (1) SCHEDULE SLIP: TechCrunch reported backer devices shipping before Christmas 2025; the current 28.5in product page says 'Expected shipping starts August 2026' — roughly an 8-month gap between backer and retail fulfilment. (2) WHEN I FETCHED ARPOBOT.COM ON 2026-08-05, THE STOREFRONT LISTED ONLY THE ARPOBOT SMART SHADE AND A BATTERY PACK — NO E-INK CANVAS OF ANY KIND. A crowdfunded 'World's First Smart COLOUR E-Ink Frame' absent from its creator's own catalogue sixteen months after the campaign closed is the signature of a discontinued or deprioritised side project. I cannot prove abandonment — the bloomin8.com domain is live and selling, and the campaign reportedly carried a July 2026 update — but the split between the two storefronts is itself a signal about where engineering attention lives.
vendors.rationale: Blunt: a Sydney crowdfunding startup on its second product, with about AU$2.4M raised, no disclosed institutional funding, an undisclosed and probably tiny headcount, and a large-format SKU that is only just reaching customers roughly 16 months after the campaign closed. Three-year survival is genuinely uncertain and the client should assume a real chance of no warranty support and no app maintenance by 2029. BUT this is the second and more important case where openness offsets fragility, and it does so more usefully than Modos because the size is actually right. The device exposes a local HTTP REST API discoverable over mDNS, the vendor publishes the Home Assistant integration that documents that API, there is an SD card slot that works with no network at all, and a genuinely diverse third-party ecosystem has already formed - 19 GitHub repositories from at least nine different authors, including a macOS desktop manager, a Node CLI with Spectra 6 dithering, a Python library, a Swift local server, LAN control tooling and a self-hosted pull endpoint. If BLOOMIN8 disappears, the frame keeps working on the LAN, the SD card path keeps working offline, and third parties have already demonstrated they can drive it without the vendor. That is a materially different and better failure mode than any closed frame at this size. The residual risk is that the API contract is documented only by vendor-published code rather than a specification, so a firmware update could break third-party tooling.

vendors.name: Bigme (Xinruizhi Technology)
vendors.corporate_form: Private company; 'Bigme' is a brand of Xinruizhi Technology. Corporate identity is fragmented — a subagent found the warranty issued by a differently named entity ('Bigme Cloud Literacy Technology Co., Ltd.') and contradictory governing-law clauses; I did not verify those, so they are unverified but worth checking if warranty enforceability matters.
vendors.ownership: Private — and notably NOT wholly independent: PocketBook International became a substantial shareholder and co-owner of Bigme in May 2024. This is a shareholding and co-ownership arrangement, not a full acquisition; the two companies cross-share R&D teams and do mutual product development (the PocketBook InkPad EO is Bigme InkNote Color+ hardware with PocketBook firmware).
vendors.funding: No VC rounds found. Growth funded through ODM work and Kickstarter launches.
vendors.revenue_scale: Not disclosed. Claims 9,000,000+ units shipped across 100+ countries and 100+ offline experience stores in China.
vendors.hardware_track_record: Parent established 2008; claims 16 years of industry experience and seven generations of colour e-ink work, with an ODM history building E Ink readers for other brands before launching its own brand around 2020. Broad catalogue — e-ink tablets, e-paper monitors, e-ink smartphones, colour e-ink all-in-one PCs — and claims the world's first 10.3in colour e-ink tablet and the first 25.3in colour e-ink all-in-one PC. Operates a first-party store, a separate Euro shop, and Amazon US.
vendors.abandonment_history: Not verified with a fetched source. The observable pattern is very high model churn plus 'world's first' marketing on multiple SKUs, which in practice tends to mean short per-model support lifetimes — inference, not finding. What IS independently documented is software and support quality: eWritable scores Bigme firmware 70% and the company 75%, criticising a 'disjointed, and even frustrating' interface, software that 'lacks maturity and can feel quite clunky and non-intuitive', variable customer support with no native English speakers and no online knowledge base, and concludes 'there are very few reasons (in my opinion) to choose Bigme over Boox'.
vendors.rationale: An 18-year manufacturing base plus a European strategic shareholder (PocketBook) is real ballast, and Bigme is the price leader at 25.3in. But the corporate identity is fragmented across differently named entities, there is no disclosed revenue or headcount, launches depend on Kickstarter, and its software and support are independently rated the weakest of the three monitor vendors. Rated medium on corporate survival while flagging that per-model firmware support is the weak point. For his purposes the software criticism matters less than it would for a tablet, because with a monitor the host does all the work — but it does mean he should not count on Bigme firmware updates fixing anything.

vendors.name: Bigme (brand of Xinruizhi Technology)
vendors.corporate_form: Bigme is a BRAND, not the legal entity. Parent per its own About page is 'Xinruizhi Technology', established 2008. Exact registered entity name and address unverified.
vendors.ownership: MATERIALLY: PocketBook International became a substantial shareholder and co-owner on 2024-05-25, with active cross-sharing of R&D teams. The exact stake percentage is NOT disclosed — primary reporting says 'substantial shareholder and co-owner' while secondary databases characterise it as majority or an acquisition; treat 'majority' as unverified.
vendors.funding: Kickstarter/Indiegogo campaigns (inkNote and Galy reportedly raised about US$1.2m combined, and about $800k for a Kaleido 3 tablet — both unverified), plus the PocketBook investment.
vendors.revenue_scale: Not disclosed
vendors.hardware_track_record: About 18 years as an ODM but only 6 under its own brand: white-label ODM for other brands 2009-2017 and still their sole R&D centre; Bigme brand launched 2020. Self-reported 100+ countries and 9,000K+ cumulative shipments. Genuine silicon and firmware capability — among the deepest in the consumer set. >15in products: B251 (25.3in Kaleido 3, 3200x1800, launched on Kickstarter in monitor and all-in-one-PC forms, tiers $1,299-$1,999, retail list $1,999 monitor / $2,999 AIO) and B251 Pro (25.3in, 3200x1800 Kaleido 3, 4,096 colours, HDMI + DisplayPort, USB-C for firmware updates only, 'up to 60 FPS', list $1,599, street $1,279-$1,349, delivery from about 2026-07-10). 1-year warranty.
vendors.abandonment_history: FIRMWARE IS BIGME'S DOCUMENTED WEAKEST DIMENSION. An independent reviewer scores its firmware 70%, describing the UI as 'quite disjointed, and even frustrating to use at times', and notes support via email/WhatsApp/Skype with variable response times and language-barrier friction. Bigme also ships many models per year with DIVERGENT FIRMWARE VERSION TREES PER DEVICE — a classic long-term-support smell. At least one report exists of a malfunctioning B251 monitor where firmware fixes failed and a return was refused. Its Galy was the ACeP/Gallery 3 device that E Ink's panel-generation retreat discontinued, so Bigme has already been on the losing end of an E Ink panel decision once. The 25.3in monitor is a first-generation 2026 product whose 'up to 60 FPS' claim has no independent measurement; a reviewer is explicitly sceptical, noting that manufacturer speed claims describe the best case and that fast modes imply aggressive waveform optimisation with reduced greyscale and colour quality, visible artifacts and increased ghosting. USB-C on the B251 Pro is firmware-update-only, not video — a hardware-level dependency on continued firmware publication from the vendor whose firmware is the known weak point. No discontinued-cloud incidents, layoffs or insolvency found.
vendors.distributor_footprint: Own stores (store.bigme.vip, euroshop.bigme.vip, bigmestore.com), Amazon presence, Kickstarter/Indiegogo, plus the PocketBook channel into Europe via co-developed SKUs.
vendors.rationale: Bigme is a contract manufacturer that started badging its own products six years ago and is now selling a first-generation 25.3in monitor on an unmeasured refresh-rate claim, with firmware quality as its lowest-rated attribute and a USB-C port whose only purpose is receiving firmware from that same vendor. Without PocketBook this would be a low. The PocketBook stake — a 19-year-old Swiss-domiciled e-reader house with a real European channel and shared R&D — is the only thing that makes the three-year survival bet reasonable, and it also provides a plausible continuity path if Bigme stumbles. But note the concentration point again: choosing Bigme over InkPoster is not diversification, because PocketBook sits behind both. Also note for scope: Bigme has NO qualifying art-frame product — every frame-shaped Bigme device is 13.3in or smaller, and the only >15in offering is a computer monitor.

Do not treat CLEARink as an E Ink alternative, and treat any future claim of an E Ink competitor with the scepticism this case earns.

vendors.name: DASUNG Tech Co., Ltd.
vendors.country: China — BEIJING (Haidian District, Zhongguancun). NOTE: not Guangzhou; the FCC-filing and D&B name is Beijing Dasung Tech Co., Ltd.
vendors.corporate_form: Private limited company, founded March 2014
vendors.ownership: Private. Founder credited as the science-fiction writer 'Gong Gu'er' / Dong Gong. A founding trio including Dr. Ray Chen and Hiro Gong is reported but unverified.
vendors.funding: NO VERIFIED ROUND. Reported angel funding with CAS Star as investor — unverified. What the company publishes INSTEAD of investors is a list of Chinese government and industrial-policy designations: national high-tech enterprise, Beijing 'Specialized, Sophisticated, Distinctive and Innovative' SME, Innovative SME, Gazelle Enterprise, Zhongguancun High-Tech Enterprise, Zhongguancun Golden Seed Enterprise. Read that as a subsidy-and-grant-supported SME, not a VC-backed company.
vendors.revenue_scale: Unknown — not disclosed anywhere fetchable
vendors.headcount: Not disclosed on the vendor site. A LinkedIn self-reported band of 51-200 employees was found by a subagent; I did not fetch it, so unverified.
vendors.hardware_track_record: Founded March 2014; about 12 years building e-ink monitors specifically, and it effectively created the category. Product history: Paperlike (mono monitor), Paperlike Color, Not-eReader tablet, Link (e-ink phone display). Claims coverage by 300+ media outlets in 20+ languages and users in 80+ countries — though country counts vary between its own pages (80+, 78, 65). Direct-to-consumer from Beijing; no published distributor or authorised-reseller network.
vendors.abandonment_history: SEVERAL CONCRETE PROBLEMS. (1) THE LAUNCH MODEL IS CROWDFUNDING, REPEATEDLY: Indiegogo campaigns for Paperlike 3, Paperlike HD, Paperlike Pro Touch, an e-ink monitor in 2021, Paperlike Color (estimated shipping December 2023 at $1,529/$1,599 perks) and Paperlike 13K. A vendor that funds each new flagship by pre-selling it has no balance-sheet cushion for a bad cycle. (2) THE FLAGSHIP 25.3IN IS LISTED SOLD OUT on Dasung's own store at $1,549 as of 2026-08-05 — the exact SKU in the buyer's size class is not currently purchasable first-party. (3) THE US DISTRIBUTOR DOES NOT CARRY IT: SOL Computer, the certified US distributor, stocks only 10.3in and 13.3in models ($449-$899). There is NO 25.3in Dasung in the US channel, so RMA on a >15in unit goes back to Beijing. (4) PLATFORM SUPPORT ACTIVELY DROPPED: the Paperlike 253 client software supports Apple M1-M4 only and explicitly NOT Intel Macs; Linux gets extended-display mode only. (5) A REPORTED HARDWARE-GATED FIRMWARE CUTOFF: a free firmware upgrade for the 25.3in Paperlike Color was made available only to units manufactured from October 2025 onward 'due to hardware limitations' (unverified) — if true, the same SKU is already forked into supported and unsupported populations. (6) First-generation Paperlike (2015) shipped with unfinished drivers and some units died within months (unverified); counterpoint from first-hand user reports, a 2018 HD unit ran 8 hours a day for 18 months with no degradation and an early-2016 unit was still functional. Dasung has acknowledged that video playback accelerates panel deterioration. No published RMA depot outside Beijing; support is an email address. No layoffs or insolvency found.
vendors.rationale: Twelve years of continuous shipping and real category-defining IP, but bluntly: an opaque, small, grant-supported SME that funds flagships by pre-selling them, discloses no headcount or revenue, keeps its largest product out of its own US channel, currently shows that product sold out, and has apparently already split the 25.3in line into firmware-supported and unsupported manufacture dates. They will probably still exist in three years. Whether the client's SPECIFIC 253 unit still receives firmware is a materially weaker and different bet — and with no US RMA path for a $1,549 display, a panel failure in year two means freight to Beijing. As with Onyx, the architectural upside is real: it is an HDMI monitor, so his app can drive it with no cloud. The art-specific downside is the same Kaleido 3 desaturation, or no colour at all on the mono version.

vendors.name: Dalian Good Display Co., Ltd.
vendors.corporate_form: Limited company. Registered capital, shareholders and revenue NOT OBTAINABLE — Chinese registry aggregators returned redirects or HTTP 410 and epaper-china.com does not resolve.
vendors.ownership: Private. Operates good-display.com plus retail fronts buy-lcd.com and buyepaper.com (which 302-redirects to buy-lcd.com), and is linked to several further domains. No parent, shareholders, listing or financials disclosed on any page I fetched.
vendors.funding: No funding rounds found
vendors.revenue_scale: Not obtainable
vendors.hardware_track_record: A long-standing E Ink module house — roughly 19 years (site footer runs from 2007) — with a very large catalogue from tiny segment displays up to 42in, matching driver boards and TCON boards (DEAM-315E1, DEJA-TC103, 31.2in large-size driver boards), downloadable datasheets with visible download counters, Arduino-compatible code examples, and its own e-commerce channel selling both bare modules and finished displays worldwide. It sells the same 31.5in Spectra 6 panel that Samsung, Philips and PocketBook build into products, so it sits directly in the E Ink supply chain rather than reselling finished goods.
vendors.abandonment_history: Not researched. Two caveats about character rather than abandonment. First, documentation and commerce quality: prices frequently absent, stock thin (the 31.5in finished unit showed '0 in stock'), specs internally inconsistent on the retail front (2560x1440 versus a claimed '3200x1800 effective resolution' on the same listing), support via email enquiry. Second — a finding I flag as unverified because I did not fetch the relevant pages myself — a subagent reports that Good Display makes NO claim of authorised-partner, licensee or distributor status with E Ink, and that E Ink's own partner ecosystem listing does not name Good Display, which would make it an unaffiliated downstream converter buying E Ink film on ordinary commercial terms. I can confirm the second half directly: the E Ink company page I fetched names PPDS/Philips, Sharp, AUO Display Plus, MediaTek and others, and does not name Good Display.
vendors.rationale: Good Display is the real engineering entity behind a large slice of the hobby and OEM e-paper market — the GDE part numbers, waveforms and driver code originate here, so there is genuine design depth rather than pure rebadging, and their 42in part is one of the very few routes to an E Ink panel above 32 inches. But you cannot underwrite a three-year firmware commitment from a company with no accessible accounts, no disclosed ownership and no registered capital figure. Treat as a component supplier to second-source, never as a platform partner. For this client the practical relevance is as a bare-panel route if he wants to build a frame himself — and if he goes that way, buy from Good Display directly rather than through a reseller.

vendors.name: Dalian Good Display Co., Ltd. (storefront: buy-lcd.com)
vendors.corporate_form: Private limited company (Co., Ltd.)
vendors.ownership: Private; not disclosed. Widely understood to be associated with the DKE brand, though that link was not verified in this session.
vendors.funding: Not disclosed
vendors.revenue_scale: Not disclosed
vendors.hardware_track_record: Deep and specifically relevant: the most complete catalogue of large-format e-paper panels, driver boards, TCON boards, development kits and finished signage found anywhere in this survey. Sizes from 1.69 in round through 4 in, 5.9 in, 7.3 in, 13.3 in, 25.3 in, 28.5 in and 31.5 in, plus finished poster products (DMPH253E61, DMPH315E61), development kits (DEAM-315E1, ESP32-133C02, ESP32E6-E01, DEJA-TC103), a 31.2 in Android motherboard plus TCON plus power-supply set, and Windows tooling (XTacepSetup v25.02.25). Publishes downloadable specification sheets with download counters, and example code libraries for STM32, ESP32, Arduino and Raspberry Pi with documentation for controllers from Solomon, UltraChip, JADARD, IST, Himax, ITE, Sitronix and Fudan Micro. Operates its own e-commerce storefront at buy-lcd.com with real listed prices.
vendors.abandonment_history: Product lines are actively retired - the 25.3 in monochrome signage DMPH253EG1 is explicitly marked [EOL] on their site. That is a normal supplier practice, but it is direct evidence that a specific panel or product the client standardises on may become unavailable, which matters for spares over a multi-year build.
vendors.rationale: Rated medium on track record and catalogue depth rather than on any verifiable financial evidence, of which there is none - no financials, no headcount, no ownership, no ticker. What justifies medium is that this is plainly an established, operating distributor and module house with an enormous documented catalogue, published datasheets, its own priced storefront, multi-platform code libraries and long-standing relationships across the E Ink controller ecosystem. It is not a startup and not a one-product vendor. Two specific cautions for the client. FIRST, most interesting items were out of stock when surveyed (GDEP253C02 at USD 898.20, DMPH315E61 at USD 1,636.20, both 0 in stock) and several large-panel pages carry no price at all or are unpopulated stubs (GDES285E01), so procurement is a made-to-order conversation with lead-time risk, not a click-to-buy. SECOND, the documented EOL of a 25.3 in product line is a real warning about long-term spares. WHY THIS VENDOR MATTERS MOST FOR A SELF-BUILD: it is the only supplier from which a determined builder can buy the >15 in panel, the TCON, the Android motherboard, the power-supply board and the Windows image-packaging tool as a coherent set, with an SDK, and with published prices for some items. If the client goes the bare-panel route, this is the counterparty.

vendors.name: Digital View Limited / Digital View Inc.
vendors.country: United Kingdom, United States (Morgan Hill, California) and Hong Kong
vendors.corporate_form: DIGITAL VIEW LIMITED, CH 03009112, incorporated 1995-01-12, ACTIVE, SIC 26512, registered office The Estate Office, Knebworth Park, Hertfordshire SG3 6PY. Accounts to 2024-12-31, next due 2026-09-30, confirmation statement 2025-10-31, NO OVERDUE FILINGS. Sister entity DIGITAL VIEW GROUP LIMITED (04376204), incorporated 2002-02-18, active, same address.
vendors.ownership: CLEAN AND UNCHANGED FOR 30 YEARS: PSCs are Richard Stucley Fromanteel Lytton Cobbold (British, UK) and James Henry (British, resident Hong Kong), each 25-50% of shares and voting rights, both notified 2016-04-06, BOTH STILL ACTIVE, NEITHER CEASED. The two founders still control the company. Two known active shareholders.
vendors.funding: NONE. No VC, no PE, no exit event.
vendors.revenue_scale: Not disclosed — Northdata premium-gated, and the company publishes no figures.
vendors.hardware_track_record: 31 YEARS of display controller electronics — founded March 1995 in England and Hong Kong by James Henry and Richard Cobbold, expanding to California within a year. 'Engineering display electronics since 1995.' >15in capability is the broadest of any vendor here: TCON driver boards for E Ink panels FROM 13.3IN TO 75IN, mono and colour, plus indoor and outdoor monitors and kits, plus image-transfer software for E Ink displays. Its 32in Outdoor E-Paper Display (V32-OSM) — 31.2in reflective E Ink, 2560x1440, up to 16 greys, IP65 and IK8, aluminium enclosure with AR-treated optically bonded cover glass, built-in front light, VESA 200x200, portrait or landscape, USB image interface — IS SOLD THROUGH E INK'S OWN SHOPKITS STORE, i.e. E Ink itself fronts the product. Range described as 13.3in to 84in IP-65 outdoor.
vendors.abandonment_history: NONE FOUND — no insolvency, no restructuring, no discontinued-platform notices, and no ownership change in 30 years. Its core markets (industrial, medical, marine, transportation) structurally reward long product availability and punish EOL churn.
vendors.distributor_footprint: Industrial/commercial channels plus, notably, E Ink's own shopkits webshop — a meaningful vote of confidence from the panel maker and one of the few routes by which a small buyer can obtain a large-format e-paper product through E Ink's channel.
vendors.rationale: THE BEST CONTINUITY PROFILE AMONG THE BOUTIQUE VENDORS and the one I would trust most for long-tail firmware: founder-owned since 1995, no investor clock forcing an exit, no filing delinquency in 30 years, and a customer base that punishes end-of-life churn. Being carried in E Ink's own store is real third-party validation. Its TCON driver boards spanning 13.3in to 75in are also, for a client building his own frame, probably the single most useful commercial product in this entire survey — it is the controller layer that turns a bare E Ink panel into something his app can push images to. Offsetting: a small, private, financially opaque controller-board house with no published revenue or headcount, so bus-factor and customer concentration are unquantifiable — hence medium rather than higher. And be precise about what they are: DIGITAL VIEW MAKES THE TCON AND THE ENCLOSURE, NOT THE PANEL. Their own 32in product is monochrome 16-grey, unusable for colour art — but their controller boards support colour panels up to 75in, which is the interesting part.

vendors.corporate_form: Public company
vendors.ownership: Publicly listed on the Taipei Exchange
vendors.funding: Not applicable — listed company
vendors.public_ticker: 8069 (Taipei Exchange / TPEX), confirmed on E Ink's own corporate page and market data
vendors.revenue_scale: FY2025 revenue NT$36.12 billion, up 12.29% YoY and the highest in 14 years; net profit NT$10.52bn, up 18.6% from NT$8.87bn in 2024; EPS NT$9.14 (TTM 9.58). Gross margin ~50-54%, ROCE 60-100%. Market cap NT$225.29bn, PE 20.41, dividend yield 2.99%. Revenue trajectory 2021 NT$19.65bn → 2022 NT$30.06bn → 2023 NT$27.12bn (a real 9.8% decline) → 2024 NT$32.16bn → 2025 NT$36.12bn. R&D roughly USD 150m/yr, mid-teens percent of revenue.
vendors.headcount: 777 per market data — I am flagging this as probably a parent-entity or registrant figure rather than group headcount, since it is implausibly low for a multi-fab group, and eink.com's own IR page states no headcount.
vendors.hardware_track_record: Self-described 'originator, pioneer, and commercial leader in ePaper technology', with market share in the high 90s across e-readers, electronic shelf labels and signage — the brand name is the category name. Named subsidiary Linfiny Japan Inc. Included in the Dow Jones Sustainability World Index and DJSI Emerging Markets for three consecutive years, ranked top company in Electronic Equipment, Instruments & Components worldwide, top 2% in CDP 2024, SBTi-validated targets, RE100. Sells developer panels direct via shopkits.eink.com. AGGRESSIVE CAPACITY INVESTMENT, which is the most relevant durability signal for a 3-year plan: 2026 capex NT$5-8bn versus NT$5bn in 2025; the H5 line — the first dedicated to large 32in and 55in displays — entered volume production late 2025; H6 launches at Hsinchu Science Park in 2026 and contributes revenue in 2027; further expansion at Taoyuan's Guanyin District and in the United States. Chairman Johnson Lee: 'I am bullish about this market, so we have to keep expanding capacity.' ESL volumes projected at 600m units in 2026, up 20%, with Walmart, Lidl and Tesco named as customers.
vendors.abandonment_history: Not researched directly. Two relevant patterns: E Ink renames and re-generations its colour technologies quickly (ACeP / Advanced Colour, Gallery 3, Kaleido 1-3, Spectra 3000/3100/6), so panel generations turn over faster than a 3-year product plan — the Philips 25in already runs a superseded colour generation. And the core microencapsulated-electrophoretic patent, filed in the late 1990s by MIT researchers, EXPIRED IN 2018, so the moat is now know-how, scale and continuous innovation rather than IP.
vendors.rationale: THE LOAD-BEARING VENDOR IN THIS SURVEY, and the right one to depend on. Every device here — Samsung, Philips, InkPoster, BOOX, DASUNG, Bigme, Visionect, Good Display, Papercast, Modos — is downstream of E Ink panel supply. Financially it is in excellent shape: record 2025 revenue and profit, ~50% gross margins, equity roughly triple debt (NT$65.7bn vs NT$23.1bn), NT$20bn cash, and NT$5-8bn of 2026 capex across four expansion fronts including a line purpose-built for large panels. The risk is not E Ink's survival but everyone's concentration on it: high-90s share with no alternative supplier at these sizes, a documented precedent of being fully booked (2022), and a core patent that lapsed in 2018 without Chinese rivals yet achieving volume or comparable quality. Buying panels direct from shopkits.eink.com is the practical hedge available to him.
